screens.title: Building User Interfaces with React Native Components
screens.subtitle: Use core components, Flexbox, and StyleSheet to create native-feeling mobile layouts

narration.text: In this lesson you'll learn the essential building blocks of user interfaces in React Native. We focus on the core components—View, Text, Image, and Button—and how they map to native platform elements so your app feels and performs like a native experience. You'll also learn to position and size components using Flexbox, and to author styles with StyleSheet for maintainability and performance. I'll show concrete examples and a hands-on activity to build a profile card. These skills matter because React Native doesn't use H T M L; you compose native components via JavaScript, and understanding how layout and styling differ from the web prevents common errors such as leaving text unwrapped or applying C S S units incorrectly. As you move through the screens, watch code examples run, practice Flexbox alignment, and complete a simple profile card layout using StyleSheet. By the end you'll know which component to choose for content, how to align items across axes, and how to structure styles for reuse. Consider: what difference will using View and Text make compared with using H T M L tags when you target iOS and Android?

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: React Native UI is composed of core components mapped to native widgets; Flexbox and StyleSheet are the primary tools for layout and styling.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These learning objectives guide your practice as you build mobile UIs with React Native. First, you'll identify and use fundamental core components: know when to pick View, Text, Image, and Button and how each corresponds to native controls. Second, you'll apply Flexbox to position and size elements across screen sizes, understanding main and cross axes with practical alignments. Third, you'll author styles using StyleSheet. create and inline styles, learning why StyleSheet can be more efficient and easier to reuse. Fourth, you'll assemble a simple responsive screen that includes text, an image, and horizontal buttons, demonstrating layout, accessibility labels, and touchable interactions. Each objective includes a practical rationale: choosing the correct component improves performance and accessibility; mastering Flexbox prevents layout surprises across devices; using StyleSheet helps keep styles predictable and reduces bridge traffic to native. A short mnemonic such as CORE = Components, Orientation, Reuse, Efficiency can help you remember the sequence of concerns when designing a screen. These objectives set the scope for hands-on work and assessment and will be verified when you build the profile card activity.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Skills & Why They Matter
screens.subtitle: Concrete skills, everyday relevance, and a quick diagnostic for each objective

narration.text: Let's connect each objective to a practical scenario so you know exactly when to use the skills. For core components: when you need fixed text or user-facing labels, use Text—not View—because Text ensures correct measurement, accessibility roles, and native rendering. Example: a user name label must be in Text to adjust font scaling. For Flexbox: when you want a row of buttons to stay evenly spaced across devices, use a container with flexDirection set to row and justifyContent to space-around. This avoids hard-coded widths and keeps UIs adaptive. For StyleSheet: prefer StyleSheet. create when styles are reused across renders; it helps with validation and reduces the cost of repeatedly sending long style objects to native. For building a responsive screen: practice combining all three. Create a centered card with an image, name, bio, and two buttons that adapt to portrait and landscape. A common diagnostic is the unwrapped text bug—if text renders unexpectedly on Android or truncates, verify it’s inside a Text component. These practical checks will help you avoid frequent mistakes while building real mobile screens.

screens.title: Core Components: View, Text, Image, Button
screens.subtitle: Understand what each core component provides and why it maps to native UI

narration.text: React Native's core components are small, focused abstractions over native controls. The View component acts as a general-purpose container. It supports layout via Flexbox, touch handling, and visual styling. When you need to group elements, add background color, borders, or arrange children, View is the right choice. The Text component is special: all textual content must be wrapped in Text; otherwise font metrics, accessibility, and line layout will behave unpredictably. For example, a user name label must be rendered with Text to support font scaling and screen readers. The Image component renders bitmap or vector images from network sources or bundled assets and offers properties for sizing and accessibility. Button is a simple, platform-agnostic control for basic interactions. For richer visuals and control over feedback you can use TouchableOpacity or Pressable; these allow styled children, animated opacity, and custom press handling. A common misconception is to treat View like a div that can directly contain text; in React Native, that leads to layout and accessibility problems. Remember: View for structure, Text for any rendered string, Image for pictures, and Button or touchables for actions. Consider how each maps to native equivalents when you aim for native look and performance.

keyIdea.title: Component roles
keyIdea.text: Use View for structure, Text for any text, Image for pictures, and Button or touchables for actions to ensure native behavior and accessibility.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Core Components
What each component does
View
Container for layout and interaction. Supports Flexbox, background, borders, and touch handling. Maps to UIView and android.view.View.
Text
All text must be wrapped in Text for correct rendering, accessibility, and font metrics. Think of it as the only place strings belong.
Image
Displays images from network or local assets. Use accessibilityLabel and explicit size to avoid layout jumps.
Button / Touchables
Button provides basic cross-platform behavior. Use TouchableOpacity or Pressable when you need custom styling or interaction feedback.
Key Takeaway

Pick components by role: structure, text, media, or interaction. This choice affects accessibility and native behavior.

Concrete Example
Imagine a profile item: put avatar in Image with fixed width and height, user name in Text, bio in Text, and a Follow button using TouchableOpacity to style rounded corners. This arrangement ensures the name scales with system fonts and the avatar reserves layout space.
Common mistake
Placing raw strings directly inside View. Always wrap strings in Text to avoid rendering and accessibility issues.
Pro tip
Use accessibilityLabel on images and touchables so screen readers announce meaningful information, like "Jane Doe profile photo".

Read the code carefully: React Native elements look similar to JSX but they map to native widgets at runtime. In practice, you'll often move inline style objects into StyleSheet. create to improve readability and performance. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Minimal App.js
Code (read-only)
<!-- App.js --> import React from 'react'; import { StyleSheet, Text, View, Image, Button, Alert } from 'react-native'; export default function App() { const imageUrl = 'https://reactnative.dev/img/tiny_logo.png'; const handlePress = () => { Alert.alert('Hello!', 'You pressed the button!'); }; return ( <View style={styles.container}> <Text style={styles.header}>Welcome to My App!</Text> <Image source={{ uri: imageUrl }} style={styles.logo} accessibilityLabel="React Native Logo" /> <Text style={styles.description}>This is a simple demonstration of core React Native UI components.</Text> <Button title="Press Me" onPress={handlePress} color="#841584" /> </View> ); } const styles = StyleSheet.create({ container: { flex: 1, backgroundColor: '#fff', alignItems: 'center', justifyContent: 'center', padding: 20 }, header: { fontSize: 24, fontWeight: 'bold', marginBottom: 15 }, logo: { width: 100, height: 100, marginBottom: 20 }, description: { fontSize: 16, textAlign: 'center', marginHorizontal: 20, marginBottom: 30 }, });
Explanation & Example
The container uses flex:1 so it fills available screen space and centers children. Image explicitly defines width and height to avoid layout reflow. Button uses a simple alert to show press handling. Accessibility is improved by adding accessibilityLabel to the Image.
Misconception to avoid
Do not use CSS units like 'px'. React Native expects numbers that represent density-independent pixels; supplying strings with units will not work as on the web.
Try this

Replace Button with TouchableOpacity and add a custom style to practice custom touch feedback.

screens.title: Flexbox Basics for React Native
screens.subtitle: Main axis, cross axis, and the properties that control alignment

narration.text: Flexbox is the primary layout system in React Native and understanding its axes is essential. In React Native the default flexDirection is column, which places children vertically; when you switch flexDirection to row, the main axis becomes horizontal. justifyContent aligns items along the main axis, for example centering a vertical stack or distributing items in a row. alignItems aligns along the cross axis, which is horizontal when flexDirection is column and vertical when flexDirection is row. The flex property controls how a component grows to fill available space: flex:1 lets a child expand to fill remaining area. A typical process when laying out a screen is: 1) decide the overall direction using flexDirection; 2) reserve major regions with container Views set to flex ratios; 3) use justifyContent to distribute space and alignItems to align cross-axis; 4) test on portrait and landscape to ensure responsiveness. A common mistake is applying justifyContent when you meant alignItems; visualize main and cross axes and label them while designing. Practicing this four-step process will reduce layout surprises and make UIs predictable across devices. Flexbox Basics for React Native means follow a four-step process: choose axis, reserve regions, distribute along main axis, align cross axis; visualize main vs cross axes to avoid mistakes.. In practical terms, main axis, cross axis, and the properties that control alignment. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Flexbox process
keyIdea.text: Follow a four-step process: choose axis, reserve regions, distribute along main axis, align cross axis; visualize main vs cross axes to avoid mistakes.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Flexbox Basics
Four-step layout process
1
Choose axis
Decide whether children flow vertically (column) or horizontally (row).
2
Reserve regions
Use nested Views with flex ratios to allocate header, body, and footer space.
3
Distribute main-axis
Use justifyContent to align children along the main axis (space-between, center, space-around).
4
Align cross-axis
Use alignItems to position children on the cross axis (stretch, center, flex-start).
Concrete example
To center a login form vertically, set the container to flex:1 and justifyContent:'center'. To center inputs horizontally as well, add alignItems:'center'.
Visual reminder
Main axis: direction items flow (depends on flexDirection). Cross axis: perpendicular to main axis.
flex: controls how much a child grows to fill available space. A child with flex:1 will expand.
Key Takeaway

Always label axes in your head: if you know the main axis, justifyContent and alignItems become predictable tools.

Common mistake
Applying justifyContent when you meant alignItems. If items move in the wrong direction, check which axis is active.

screens.title: justifyContent vs alignItems
screens.subtitle: How the two alignment properties behave across axes

narration.text: Understanding justifyContent and alignItems is easier when you compare their effects. When flexDirection is column, justifyContent controls vertical distribution while alignItems controls horizontal alignment. For example, in a vertical list justifyContent:'space-between' will push the first and last items to the top and bottom of the container; alignItems:'center' will center each child horizontally. When flexDirection is row, their roles flip: justifyContent affects horizontal spacing and alignItems controls vertical placement. A practical example: to create a centered toolbar across the bottom of the screen, set container flexDirection to row, justifyContent to space-around to distribute buttons, and alignItems to center so they line up vertically. A frequent misconception is assuming they both move items the same way regardless of flexDirection. The contrast is that justifyContent distributes free space along the main axis, alignItems positions children along the cross axis. Comparing small test containers and changing flexDirection instantly clarifies behavior. Try swapping directions in your emulator and observe which property moves which axis. justifyContent vs alignItems means justifycontent distributes space on the main axis; alignitems positions on the cross axis. their effect changes when flexdirection switches.. In practical terms, how the two alignment properties behave across axes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Alignment contrast
keyIdea.text: justifyContent distributes space on the main axis; alignItems positions on the cross axis. Their effect changes when flexDirection switches.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › justifyContent vs alignItems
Compare scenarios
Column (default)
Main axis: vertical. justifyContent affects vertical spacing; alignItems controls horizontal alignment.
Row
Main axis: horizontal. justifyContent affects horizontal spacing; alignItems controls vertical alignment.
Example question
You want three buttons evenly spaced across the bottom of the screen. Set flexDirection:'row' and justifyContent:'space-around'. Use alignItems:'center' so buttons sit on the same vertical level.
Quick test card
Check: swap flexDirection from column to row and observe which property changes alignment behavior.
Misconception: justifyContent always moves elements left/right. It does that only when the main axis is horizontal.
Key Takeaway

Label your axes mentally. Knowing the main axis clarifies which property to change.

screens.title: Structuring a Screen: Header, Body, Footer
screens.subtitle: Using nested Views and flex ratios to create predictable regions

narration.text: A reliable screen structure splits the UI into header, content, and footer regions. Use nested Views and flex ratios so each region behaves predictably across devices. For example, give header and footer fixed content sizes while assigning flex:1 to the body so it expands to fill remaining space. Within the body, further divide into columns or rows using flexDirection. This architecture prevents overlap and ensures elements stay within safe bounds when the keyboard appears or when the device rotates. Practical steps include: declare a top-level View with flex:1, create a header View without flex or with a small fixed height for titles, create a body View with flex:1 to host scrollable or flexible content, and a footer View that contains actions with flexDirection:'row' for buttons. A common pitfall is giving multiple children unnecessarily high flex values that cumulatively exceed available space; visualize proportion and test resizing. Accessibility matters here too: ensure interactive footer buttons have sufficient hit area and labels. This structure scales from simple profile cards to complex multi-section screens. Structuring a Screen: Header, Body, Footer means use a top-level flex:1 container, a non-flex header, a flex:1 body, and a footer with row buttons to create stable, responsive screens.. In practical terms, using nested views and flex ratios to create predictable regions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Screen layout pattern
keyIdea.text: Use a top-level flex:1 container, a non-flex header, a flex:1 body, and a footer with row buttons to create stable, responsive screens.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Screen Structure
Header / Body / Footer pattern
Start with a top-level container that fills the screen. Reserve space with small fixed-height header and footer Views, and give the body flex:1 so it receives remaining space. This keeps the main content flexible while stabilizing navigation and actions.
Concrete layout example
Top Title (fixed), Profile content (flex:1), Bottom action buttons (row with justifyContent:'space-around').
Accessibility note
Ensure footer buttons are at least 44x44 dp or larger for comfortable taps and include accessibilityLabel strings.
Visual sample (annotated cards)
Header: title and optional back button. Keep compact height.
Body: main content area, set flex:1. Can host scrollable lists or centered card.
Footer: action buttons in a row with adequate spacing.
Common mistake

Giving every child flex:1 makes their sizes equal but often not what you want; prefer explicit ratios for predictable layouts.

screens.title: Hierarchy and Text Rules
screens.subtitle: Nesting rules, Text wrapping, and why hierarchy matters for styling

narration.text: Hierarchy in React Native dictates how styles are applied and how children are composed. Unlike web C S S which allows text directly inside div-like elements, React Native requires that any visible string be inside a Text component. This rule ensures proper measurement and accessibility. When nesting, you can place Text inside a View or inside another Text component; nested Text components inherit certain text styles from their parent Text, enabling inline styling like bold or colored spans. Views do not pass text properties to nested Text automatically. Another important hierarchical consideration is that styles do not cascade like web C S S—each component needs explicit styles passed via the style prop or via a StyleSheet reference. This reduces accidental inheritance but means you must plan style reuse. A common pitfall is expecting global font styling to apply to all Text components; instead create a shared text style and apply it to each Text or wrap content in a higher-level Text with inherited styles. Thinking through your component hierarchy up front reduces duplication and prevents inconsistent appearance across screens. Hierarchy and Text Rules means text must be wrapped in text; styles don't cascade like css, so plan explicit style reuse or shared components for consistent typography.. In practical terms, nesting rules, text wrapping, and why hierarchy matters for styling. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Hierarchy rules
keyIdea.text: Text must be wrapped in Text; styles don't cascade like CSS, so plan explicit style reuse or shared components for consistent typography.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Hierarchy & Text Rules
Text nesting and inheritance
Text must live inside a Text component. You may nest Text inside Text for inline style overrides. Views do not inherit text styles. To keep typography consistent, create a shared style and apply it to each Text element or build a small Text wrapper component that applies the base style automatically.
Concrete example
Wrap user name in <Text> with a header style, and bio in another <Text> with smaller font size. If you need bold inline text inside a sentence, nest a child Text with fontWeight set to bold.
Style planning
Since styles don't cascade, prefer StyleSheet.create and shared style objects. This prevents duplication and ensures consistent spacing, color, and typography across components.
Common mistake

Expecting global CSS rules to apply. In React Native, apply styles explicitly or create wrapper components.

Check your understanding
If a font weight change doesn't affect a child Text, verify whether the child has a conflicting style or whether the font supports the weight on the platform.

screens.title: Styling with StyleSheet.create()
screens.subtitle: Why StyleSheet.create helps and how to refactor inline styles

narration.text: StyleSheet. create is a simple A P I that takes a plain JavaScript object of style definitions and returns a frozen object of style IDs. Using StyleSheet provides validation while authoring and can be more efficient because it allows the framework to send style references to native once instead of repeatedly sending long style objects on each render. In practice, start with inline styles while experimenting, but refactor repeated or complex styles into StyleSheet. create when you stabilize layout. Keep style property names in camelCase—React Native does not accept 'background-color'—and use numbers for dimensions, not C S S units. A concrete refactor would move button, card, and text style objects into a shared styles constant and then reference styles. button or styles. card in the JSX. This keeps components declarative and easier to read. A common misconception is that StyleSheet magically makes styles faster in every case; while it can reduce bridge traffic for large repeated objects, correct usage and avoiding unnecessary re-creation of style objects during render are what matter most. Styling with StyleSheet.create() means stylesheet.create validates and centralizes styles, and helps reduce repeated style objects sent to native when used appropriately.. In practical terms, why stylesheet.create helps and how to refactor inline styles. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: StyleSheet benefit
keyIdea.text: StyleSheet.create validates and centralizes styles, and helps reduce repeated style objects sent to native when used appropriately.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › StyleSheet.create
Refactor example
// styles example const styles = StyleSheet.create({ container: { flex: 1, alignItems: 'center', justifyContent: 'center', padding: 20 }, header: { fontSize: 24, fontWeight: 'bold' }, card: { backgroundColor: '#fff', borderRadius: 10, padding: 16, width: '90%' }, buttons: { flexDirection: 'row', justifyContent: 'space-around', width: '100%' } });
When to use StyleSheet
Use StyleSheet when styles are reused or when you want a clear separation between layout and component logic. It helps readability and can lower runtime cost when style objects are stable across renders.
Key Takeaway

Refactor repeated or complex inline styles into StyleSheet.create to centralize styles and improve maintainability.

Misconception
StyleSheet alone won't fix performance if you recreate large style objects on every render. Keep styles stable and reuse references.

screens.title: Arranging Buttons Horizontally
screens.subtitle: Create a row of action buttons that adapts to screen width

narration.text: Arranging buttons horizontally is a frequent UI pattern. To build a row of two buttons that adapts, wrap them in a container View and set its flexDirection to row. Use justifyContent to space buttons evenly—space-around or space-between often works well. Give each button a style that includes flex:1 to let them grow proportionally, and margin or padding to separate them visually. If you want the buttons to shrink on small screens, avoid fixed widths and prefer percentages or flex. For example, a buttonGroup View with width set to '80%' centers the buttons and constrains their maximum span. Accessibility considerations: ensure buttons have accessibilityLabel and adequate hit area by adding padding. A misconception is setting width on buttons and assuming they will behave the same across densities; remember units are density-independent and layout depends on available parent width. Finally, test the design in both portrait and landscape and on multiple device sizes to verify spacing and touchability. Arranging Buttons Horizontally means use a row container with flexdirection:'row', justifycontent for spacing, and flex or percentage widths for responsiveness.. In practical terms, create a row of action buttons that adapts to screen width. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Button layout
keyIdea.text: Use a row container with flexDirection:'row', justifyContent for spacing, and flex or percentage widths for responsiveness.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Button Row
Pattern: Horizontal buttons
Wrap buttons in a View with flexDirection:'row'. Use justifyContent:'space-around' or 'space-between' to control spacing. Give each button container flex:1 and horizontal margin to create breathing space.
Example: buttonContainer: { flexDirection: 'row', justifyContent: 'space-around', width: '80%' } and child buttons with flex:1 and marginHorizontal:8.
Accessibility
Make buttons at least 44 dp tall and include accessibilityLabel. Avoid tiny tap targets by adding padding to the touchable area.
Concrete Scenario
Arrange a Follow and Message button evenly across the card bottom. Use a buttonGroup with width:'100%' inside the card, and set justifyContent:'space-around' so they remain even when the card shrinks.
Key Takeaway

Prefer flexible sizing over fixed widths for buttons so they adapt across screen sizes and densities.

screens.title: Build a Profile Card — Step-by-step
screens.subtitle: Follow steps to create a centered profile card with image, texts, and two buttons

narration.text: This step-by-step activity helps you apply everything you've learned. Step one: create a top-level View with style { flex:1, justifyContent:'center', alignItems:'center' } so the card is centered on the screen. Step two: inside the container add a card View with padding, borderRadius, and width around 80 percent of the parent. Step three: add an Image for the avatar and give it explicit width and height plus borderRadius to make it round. Step four: add Text components for the user's name and bio—remember each string must be inside Text. Step five: create a buttonGroup View with flexDirection:'row' and justifyContent:'space-around', place two Button or TouchableOpacity components, and give them flex:1 with marginHorizontal. Step six: extract repeated styles into StyleSheet. create to clean up your JSX. Test the layout in portrait and landscape and verify accessibility labels on the Image and buttons. By following these steps you'll produce a responsive and accessible profile card. A small debugging tip: if the avatar jumps size, ensure width and height are numbers, not strings with units. Build a Profile Card — Step-by-step means a six-step timeline from container setup to stylesheet refactor builds a responsive, accessible profile card you can reuse.. In practical terms, follow steps to create a centered profile card with image, texts, and two buttons. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Activity roadmap
keyIdea.text: A six-step timeline from container setup to StyleSheet refactor builds a responsive, accessible profile card you can reuse.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Profile Card Activity
Six steps
  1. Create top-level container: { flex:1, justifyContent:'center', alignItems:'center' }.
  2. Add card View with padding, borderRadius, and width:'80%'.
  3. Place Image for avatar with width, height, and borderRadius to form a circle.
  4. Add Text for name and bio. Wrap each string in Text components.
  5. Create buttonGroup View: flexDirection:'row', justifyContent:'space-around'. Add two buttons with flex:1 and marginHorizontal.
  6. Refactor repeated styles into StyleSheet.create and add accessibilityLabel props.
Debug tip
If sizes flicker or images overlap, confirm numerical width/height and that parent container sizes are stable (avoid percent widths inside auto-sizing parents).
Starter template
Use the provided starter App.js in the earlier code walkthrough. Replace placeholder image URL with a test URL during development and remove before production if offline assets are needed.
Key Takeaway

Follow the steps in order: container, card, media, text, actions, refactor. This yields a stable, responsive profile card.

screens.title: Common Mistakes & Troubleshooting
screens.subtitle: A checklist of frequent errors and how to fix them

narration.text: As you build React Native UIs, you'll encounter recurring mistakes. This screen gives a troubleshooting checklist. First, unwrapped text: if you see raw strings or layout errors, ensure all text nodes are inside Text components. Second, incorrect unit usage: avoid 'px' or 'em' units; use numbers (density-independent pixels) for sizes. Third, misused Flexbox properties: if elements move unexpectedly, label the main axis and cross axis and verify whether justifyContent or alignItems is appropriate. Fourth, styling inefficiencies: creating style objects inline in render causes repeated allocations; refactor into StyleSheet. create. Fifth, accessibility oversights: images and touchables without accessibilityLabel make the app hard to use with screen readers—always provide labels that describe purpose. Sixth, fixed widths that break on different devices: prefer flex ratios or percentage widths, and test on multiple sizes. For each issue try a small change and re-run the app; incrementally changing one property at a time helps isolate the cause. Ask: which of these errors have you encountered in previous projects? content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Common Mistakes
Troubleshooting checklist
  • Text not rendering properly: ensure strings are wrapped in Text.
  • Incorrect units: use numbers for dp, avoid 'px' and 'em'.
  • Axis confusion: draw the main and cross axis when debugging Flexbox.
  • Style duplication: move repeated styles into StyleSheet.create.
  • Accessibility: add accessibilityLabel for images and touchables.
  • Fixed widths: prefer flex or percentage widths for responsiveness.
Debug approach
Change one property at a time, re-run, and observe. Use small test containers to isolate behavior and log layout boxes if necessary. Visualizing axes solves many alignment problems quickly.
Pro tip

Keep a small utilities stylesheet for margins and spacing to avoid scattered numbers and inconsistent spacing across components.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: A compact summary of the most important ideas

narration.text: Let's summarize the essential points to remember. First, core components—View, Text, Image, Button—are the building blocks and map directly to native UI widgets; choose them by role. Second, Flexbox is the layout system: remember main vs cross axis and use justifyContent and alignItems accordingly. Third, StyleSheet. create centralizes styles, provides validation, and helps avoid recreating large style objects on every render. These ideas work together: choose the right component, lay it out with Flexbox, and style it with StyleSheet. Keep accessibility in mind by using accessibilityLabel for images and touchables. Lastly, prefer flexible sizing over fixed pixels and test your layouts across device sizes. screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders to keep while coding

narration.text: To close, hold these three short reminders: 1) Always wrap visible strings in Text, because that preserves accessibility and correct layout; 2) Think in axes: decide your main and cross axis early so justifyContent and alignItems work predictably; 3) Prefer StyleSheet. create for repeated styles and avoid recreating large style objects during render. These small habits reduce bugs and improve cross-platform behavior. When you return to your code, ask yourself: did I use the right component for the job, did I plan the axes, and did I centralize styles? If the answer is yes, your UI will be more maintainable and more consistent across devices. Plan axes
